docs.title: AI Canvas Prompt Library
docs.text:
This appendix is an interactive library of 353 AI Canvas prompts, each one tested repeatedly in the dCloud lab environment. Every prompt shows how it performed in testing, so you can pick the ones most likely to give a strong, consistent answer.

How to use it

  • Search for a product, site, or problem (press / to jump to the search box).
  • Filter by product area, by consistency, or turn on ✨ Top picks — prompts that scored 4.5 or higher with High consistency.
  • Sort by recommended, highest AI grade, most consistent, or fastest response.
  • Click the copy button on any prompt, then paste it into AI Canvas or the AI Assistant.
  • Prompts with a follow-up show the next question to ask in the same canvas.
  • Values highlighted in yellow, such as <alert-id>, must be replaced with a value from your environment before you run the prompt.
  • Click ☆ to save a prompt to My favorites in this browser.
  • Tried a prompt? Click 👍 or 👎 to tell other students whether it worked for you. Votes from everyone are combined, and Sort: Students' favorites puts the best-loved prompts first. Click your vote again to remove it.
  • Found a prompt that works well? Click ➕ Share a prompt. Shared prompts are reviewed before they appear in the library with a Community badge.

Open the prompt library in a new tab

Note

AI grades and consistency ratings come from automated test runs in the dCloud lab. Actual responses will vary due to the nature of the Live Lab environment and Agentic Systems

docs.title: Appendix B: Scenarios
docs.text: Want more hands-on time with AI Canvas? This appendix contains two optional practice scenarios. Each one drops you into a realistic operational situation at a branch site, and your goal is to use AI Canvas to investigate, find every active fault condition, and build a complete root cause analysis (RCA). There are no hints, prescribed steps, or suggested prompts — you decide how to approach the problem, which makes these a great way to sharpen your prompting skills. Work through them on your own or with a partner, at your own pace. When you're finished, or if you get stuck, Appendix C: Investigation Guide walks through one worked approach for each scenario.

docs.title: Scenario 1 — Buenos Aires
docs.text:
The Situation

It is Monday morning and the Buenos Aires branch is on fire. Complaints are flooding the helpdesk — users cannot reach internal applications, VoIP calls are dropping mid-session, and the NOC dashboard is lit with alerts. A change window ran over the weekend: a new access switch was added to the floor and a firewall policy update was pushed. Nothing has been formally verified since. You have full access to the Cisco Cloud Control environment — Meraki, ThousandEyes, Catalyst SD-WAN, and AI Canvas — and no one has touched a CLI. It is your job to figure out what happened.

Your Goal

Use AI Canvas in Cisco Cloud Control to investigate the Buenos Aires site, identify every active fault condition, and produce a complete Root Cause Analysis (RCA) that you could hand to a customer.

Active Fault Conditions

There are 6 active fault conditions at this site. See if you can find all of them.

What a Strong RCA Looks Like

  • Problem statement — what is happening and where
  • Contributing factors — conditions that led to or worsened the issue
  • Root cause(s) — the underlying reason the issue occurred
  • Impact assessment — what is affected and how severely
  • Recommended remediation steps — clear, actionable next steps

Check Your Work

When you have your RCA, ask yourself:

  • Which prompts moved your investigation forward, and how did they change as you learned more?
  • How are the fault conditions related, and did you connect them into one story?
  • Does your RCA cover six fault conditions, with a clear root cause and remediation for each?
  • How would you walk a customer through this investigation in a live demo?

Stuck, or ready to compare your approach? See Appendix C: Investigation Guide for a worked example of this scenario.

docs.title: Scenario 2 — Mexico City
docs.text:
The Situation

It is Tuesday afternoon. The Mexico City branch is down — partially. The helpdesk queue is growing and the calls are frustrating because users cannot describe the problem consistently. Some things work. Some do not. Public internet is reachable. Internal applications are not. Nobody can get to the intranet. Internal hostnames are not resolving. Meanwhile, the NOC has a device that has been completely silent since last night — no management polling responses, no telemetry, nothing. Overnight, the access layer received a scheduled firmware upgrade as part of a maintenance window. Post-upgrade verification was never completed. Nobody signed off on a clean bill of health before the team went home. Now it is Tuesday afternoon, the branch is degraded, and the business is asking for answers. You have full access to Cisco Cloud Control — Meraki, ThousandEyes, and AI Canvas. No CLI access yet.

Your Goal

Use AI Canvas in Cisco Cloud Control to investigate the Mexico City site, identify every active fault condition, and produce a complete Root Cause Analysis that you could hand to a customer.

Active Fault Conditions

There are 3 active fault conditions at this site. See if you can find all of them.

What a Strong RCA Looks Like

  • Problem statement — what is happening and where
  • Contributing factors — conditions that led to or worsened the issue
  • Root cause(s) — the underlying reason the issue occurred
  • Impact assessment — what is affected and how severely
  • Recommended remediation steps — clear, actionable next steps

Check Your Work

When you have your RCA, ask yourself:

  • Which prompts moved your investigation forward, and where did you change direction?
  • What do the fault conditions have in common, and did you find the shared contributing factor?
  • Does your RCA cover all three fault conditions, with a clear root cause and remediation for each?
  • How would you walk a customer through this investigation in a live demo?

Stuck, or ready to compare your approach? See Appendix C: Investigation Guide for a worked example of this scenario.

docs.title: Appendix C: Investigation Guide
docs.text: This appendix contains a worked example investigation for each Appendix B practice scenario. Use it if you get stuck, or after you finish to compare your approach with one possible path. Each guide shows a sample prompt sequence, explains the reasoning behind each step, and shows how the fault conditions can be surfaced and connected into a complete RCA. These are not the only valid approaches — your own prompting strategy may be just as effective, or better. Return to Appendix B: Scenarios for the original scenario briefs.

docs.title: Investigation Guide — Scenario 1: Buenos Aires
docs.text:
Investigation Guide — Scenario 1: Buenos Aires

Return to the scenario brief: Appendix B — Scenario 1: Buenos Aires

Note

This guide shows one effective path through the investigation. It is not the only valid approach — you may have found the same faults through a different sequence. Use this to compare strategies, not to check a single right answer.

Overview

The Buenos Aires scenario involves six fault conditions that cascade from a single weekend change window. The key insight is that the STP instability (faults 2–4) and the ACL change (fault 1) are independent failures introduced at the same time, which makes the situation appear more complex than any single fault would. DNS (fault 5) and packet fragmentation (fault 6) are background issues that compound the user experience. A strong investigation surfaces all six and explains the relationships between them.

Sample Prompt Sequence

Start broad to establish the site's overall health posture, then narrow systematically toward each fault domain.

Prompt 1 — Establish baseline 

Are there any issues currently affecting the Buenos Aires site?
What to look for: A summary of active alerts and issues. This should surface multiple problems simultaneously and give you the shape of what you are dealing with before going deep on any one thing.

Prompt 2 — Check network reachability and WAN health 

Give me a summary of my SD-WAN network and application health.
What to look for: SD-WAN site availability, application SLA violations, and WAN link statistics. Packet fragmentation on the WAN handoff may appear here as elevated error rates or MTU-related anomalies.

Prompt 3 — Surface switching and STP events 

Are there any critical alerts affecting the Buenos Aires network?
What to look for: STP topology change notifications, Root Guard events, and port state transitions. The unmanaged switch triggering TCNs and the Root Guard activation should appear in Meraki alert history.

Prompt 4 — Validate end-to-end reachability with ThousandEyes 

Are there any anomalies in my ThousandEyes tests for the Buenos Aires site?
What to look for: Packet loss, latency spikes, and path changes from the Buenos Aires enterprise agent. ThousandEyes will show where in the path traffic is being dropped — helping you separate the STP discard issue (local, access layer) from the WAN fragmentation issue (egress path).

Prompt 5 — Investigate the access policy fault 

Show me the Meraki appliance uplink status for the Buenos Aires network.
What to look for: Uplink state and any firewall or ACL policy events logged around the change window. The ACL blocking traffic on the distribution device should be visible as a policy change event or as dropped traffic in flow logs.

Prompt 6 — Surface the DNS fault 

Are there any outages affecting my monitored services right now?
What to look for: DNS test failures or resolution timeouts from the Buenos Aires vantage point. A ThousandEyes DNS server test will show the misconfigured resolver returning no results for internal hostnames.

Follow-up correlation prompt 

Correlate the STP topology changes, Root Guard activation, and port discard events at Buenos Aires and explain the relationship between them.
What to look for: The AI should connect the unmanaged switch → superior BPDU → Root Guard trigger → port root-inconsistent state → STP discarding chain. This is the core causal thread of the scenario.

The Six Fault Conditions

# Fault How it surfaces 1 Port not forwarding — access policy ACL policy event / dropped traffic in Meraki logs around the change window 2 Root guard activated Meraki alert: Root Guard triggered on distribution uplink port 3 STP discarding packets Port state shown as root-inconsistent / discarding in switching alerts 4 STP topology changes Repeated TCN events logged; spanning tree reconvergence activity 5 Misconfigured DNS ThousandEyes DNS test failures; internal hostname resolution timing out 6 Packet fragments detected WAN link error counters; MTU mismatch on MPLS handoff interface

RCA Summary — Key Points

  • Root cause thread: The weekend change window introduced two independent faults simultaneously — an unmanaged switch that destabilised spanning tree, and an ACL misconfiguration that blocked user traffic. Neither was verified post-change.
  • STP cascade: Unmanaged switch → superior BPDU advertisement → Root Guard activated → port enters root-inconsistent/discarding state → user traffic on VLAN 10 blocked.
  • DNS: DHCP scope still points to a decommissioned server — all name resolution fails silently for hosts on the affected segment.
  • Fragmentation: MTU mismatch on the WAN handoff causes large packets to fragment on egress, degrading application performance independently of the other faults.
  • Connecting thread: All faults share a single contributing factor — the change window lacked any post-change verification process.

Return to the scenario: Appendix B — Scenario 1: Buenos Aires

docs.title: Investigation Guide — Scenario 2: Mexico City
docs.text:
Investigation Guide — Scenario 2: Mexico City

Return to the scenario brief: Appendix B — Scenario 2: Mexico City

Note

This guide shows one effective path through the investigation. It is not the only valid approach — you may have found the same faults through a different sequence. Use this to compare strategies, not to check a single right answer.

Overview

The Mexico City scenario is deceptively simple: three faults, one maintenance window, one shared contributing factor. The challenge is that the symptom pattern — public internet works, internal resources do not — naturally steers teams toward a firewall or WAN hypothesis. A strong investigation pivots quickly away from that false lead by establishing device reachability first, then working inward through the access layer before arriving at DNS as the explanation for the partial-vs-full connectivity split.

The C9300-X-Leaf-1 switch explored in Section 1 of the lab is the unreachable device at the centre of this scenario.

Sample Prompt Sequence

Prompt 1 — Inventory and reachability baseline 

Show me my Mexico City devices.
What to look for: The full device list for the site. The C9300-X-Leaf-1 should appear but will show as unreachable or have stale telemetry timestamps. This is your first fault signal and your entry point into the investigation.

Prompt 2 — Establish what is and is not working 

Are there any outages affecting my monitored services right now?
What to look for: ThousandEyes test results from the Mexico City enterprise agent. External tests (public DNS, internet HTTP) will show healthy. Internal service tests will show failures. This pattern is the key diagnostic signal that points away from WAN/firewall and toward a local DNS issue.

Prompt 3 — Triage active alerts 

Are there any critical alerts affecting the Mexico City network?
What to look for: Alert timestamps relative to the maintenance window. Access port state alerts (err-disabled ports, policy violations) and device offline events will appear here. Cross-referencing timestamps confirms these faults appeared after the firmware upgrade completed.

Prompt 4 — Check uplink health to eliminate WAN hypothesis 

Meraki appliance uplink status for the Mexico City network.
What to look for: Uplink state. If uplinks are active and healthy, this definitively steers the investigation away from WAN and firewall as root causes and toward the local access layer and DHCP/DNS configuration.

Prompt 5 — Surface the DNS fault 

Are there any anomalies in my ThousandEyes tests?
What to look for: DNS resolution failures specifically for internal hostnames. The ThousandEyes DNS server test from the Mexico City agent will show the DHCP-assigned resolver failing to answer queries for internal domains while public DNS resolves normally. This explains the partial connectivity pattern completely.

Follow-up correlation prompt 

The Mexico City C9300-X-Leaf-1 went unreachable after an overnight firmware upgrade. Can you describe its last known state and help me determine whether this is a device failure or a post-upgrade configuration issue?
What to look for: Last-seen timestamps, configuration state before and after the upgrade, and whether the device is physically reachable but management-unreachable (configuration loss) versus fully offline (hardware/power failure). The distinction matters for how the remediation is prioritised.

The Three Fault Conditions

# Fault How it surfaces 1 Unreachable device C9300-X-Leaf-1 absent from telemetry / offline in Cloud Control inventory since the maintenance window 2 Port not forwarding — access policy Access port alert events post-upgrade; ports in policy-blocked or err-disabled state preventing user traffic 3 Misconfigured DNS ThousandEyes DNS test: internal hostnames fail, public DNS resolves — DHCP scope points to wrong resolver

RCA Summary — Key Points

  • The partial connectivity pattern is the key: public internet works, internal resources do not. This pattern has exactly one explanation — DNS. The DHCP scope is pointing clients at a resolver that cannot answer internal queries.
  • The unreachable device: The C9300-X-Leaf-1 went silent post-upgrade. The investigation should determine whether the device lost its management configuration (likely) versus a hardware failure (less likely given the timing). The distinction drives the remediation path.
  • The access policy fault: A policy applied during or after the upgrade caused access ports to stop forwarding frames for affected users, compounding the outage beyond what DNS alone would explain.
  • Connecting thread: All three faults share one contributing factor — the maintenance window closed without any post-upgrade verification. A verification checklist would have caught all three before business hours.

Return to the scenario: Appendix B — Scenario 2: Mexico City

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
In this lab, you experienced Cisco Cloud Control end-to-end — from exploring the platform to building on it. You navigated the unified operational environment, the 9-Dot Menu, and the inventory that ties every Cisco platform together, then worked alongside AI agents in AI Canvas to investigate cross-domain issues and reach a root cause.

From there, you explored how Cloud Control delivers value across the estate:

  • Identity — you reviewed identity posture in Identity Intelligence and saw human identities, non-human identities, applications, and endpoints come together in one view.
  • Splunk Secure Networking App — you navigated the five secure-networking pillars and saw how correlated telemetry shows where the network is healthy and where it is exposed.
  • Studio — you built and tested an AI agent with Agent Builder and generated a working application with App Builder, all governed by AI Defense guardrails.
  • Cloud Control and Cisco IQ — you followed a device from an inventory insight into Cisco IQ, planned for quantum readiness, and used AI Canvas to turn a hardening finding into remediation guidance and a Cisco Workflows action.

Value realization: together, these capabilities turn the Cisco investments customers already own into measurable outcomes — risks found sooner, issues resolved faster with shared context, and new agents and apps built on the same trusted platform.

As a next step, keep practicing. Use the AI Canvas Prompt Library to find, rate, and share prompts that work well, try the optional practice scenarios in Appendices B and C, and think about the value story you would tell a customer for each section of this lab. The more you work with AI Canvas, Studio, and Cisco IQ, the more confidently you will be able to show customers what Cisco Cloud Control can do for them.

docs.title: The Vision: Cisco Cloud Control
docs.text:
Enterprise IT runs on specialized products, each built to solve a different operational challenge. Cisco has spent decades building deep capabilities across networking, security, compute, observability, and collaboration. That depth matters — but the hardest operational problems rarely stay within one product or IT domain. Issues spill across boundaries, context gets lost, and teams spend more time coordinating than resolving.

Cisco Cloud Control was built to change that. It connects the full Cisco estate and third-party systems into one unified operational environment, giving teams a single place to manage infrastructure, carry context across products, and move from issue to resolution — without giving up the specialized tools they already rely on.

As AI agents become a practical part of IT operations, teams will increasingly work alongside agents that investigate issues, recommend changes, and take action. This new operating model is AgenticOps. Cisco Cloud Control is the platform that makes it practical — providing the trusted access, live operational context, authorized tools, and safeguards that agents need to act with confidence.

Built on this foundation, AI Canvas brings operators and AI agents together to investigate and resolve cross-domain issues in real time. Agent Builder lets organizations build their own custom agents, encode their expertise, and connect the tools they already use — such as ServiceNow, Meraki, and more.

Cisco Cloud Control delivers three foundational capabilities:

  • Manage — One control plane to manage the Cisco estate and connected third-party systems.
  • Resolve — Find and fix issues across products and IT domains with shared operational context.
  • Extend — Build custom apps and agents, connect existing tools, and add Cisco and ecosystem capabilities.

docs.title: What You Will Do in This Lab
docs.text:
In this hands-on lab you will experience Cisco Cloud Control end-to-end, moving from exploring the platform to building on it:

  1. Explore the Lab and Cloud Control Capabilities — Navigate Cisco Cloud Control and get familiar with the unified operational environment, the 9-Dot Menu, and the inventory that ties every platform together.

  2. Experience the Agentic AI Canvas — See how operators and AI agents collaborate in AI Canvas to investigate and resolve cross-domain issues across your infrastructure.

  3. Identity — Use Identity Intelligence to review your posture score and see how human identities, non-human identities, applications, and endpoints come together in one view.

  4. Splunk Secure Networking App — Explore Splunk Secure Networking Essentials and its five secure-networking pillars, from Zero Trust Access to Agentic Ops.

  5. Studio — Build and test an AI agent with Agent Builder and generate a working application with App Builder, all governed by AI Defense guardrails.

  6. Cloud Control and Cisco IQ — Follow a device from an inventory insight into Cisco IQ, plan for quantum readiness, and use AI Canvas to explain and remediate a hardening risk.

When you finish, keep going: the AI Canvas Prompt Library is an interactive library of tested AI Canvas prompts you can search, rate, and copy, and Appendices B and C offer optional practice scenarios for anyone who wants more hands-on time solving real problems with AI Canvas.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Navigate Cisco Cloud Control and explain how its unified inventory, 9-Dot Menu, and insights bring the Cisco estate into one operational view.
  • Use AI Canvas with Default and Reasoning modes to investigate cross-domain issues and work through a root cause analysis.
  • Assess identity posture in Identity Intelligence, including users, applications, endpoints, AI agents, and non-human identities.
  • Interpret the Splunk Secure Networking Essentials dashboards across the five secure-networking pillars, from Zero Trust Access to Agentic Ops.
  • Build and test an AI agent with Agent Builder and generate an application with App Builder, and explain how AI Defense governs what Studio builds.
  • Trace a device from a Cloud Control inventory insight into Cisco IQ to evaluate quantum readiness, certificate expiry, and security hardening findings.
  • Use AI Canvas to turn Cisco IQ findings into device-specific remediation guidance and a review-ready Cisco Workflows action.
  • Find, rate, and share effective AI Canvas prompts with the AI Canvas Prompt Library to build stronger customer demos.

docs.title: Section 1: Explore the LAB and Cloud Control Capabilities
Section 1: Explore the LAB and Cloud Control Capabilities
docs.text: In this section, you will discover how Cloud Control streamlines the management of your cloud infrastructure through a centralized interface. You'll gain hands-on experience with its core monitoring, automation, and governance features to understand how they work together to simplify operations at scale.

docs.title: Lab Topology
docs.text:
Your lab environment is pre-integrated with a broad set of Cisco platforms and services. The topology reflects a realistic enterprise deployment, giving you visibility and control across networking, security, cloud, and collaboration domains.

The following products and controllers are available in your environment:

  • Cisco Security Cloud Control — The unified management plane that ties all security services together.

  • AI Defense — Provides AI-powered threat detection and policy enforcement across your environment.

  • Multicloud Defense — Delivers consistent security policy and visibility across multiple cloud providers.

  • Secure Access — A cloud-delivered SSE solution combining ZTNA, SWG, CASB, and DNS security.

  • Secure Firewall — Next-generation firewall capabilities managed through the unified control plane.

  • Secure Workload — Provides workload segmentation, micro-segmentation policy, and application dependency mapping.

  • Cisco Meraki — Cloud-managed networking including switching, wireless, and SD-WAN, integrated directly into Cloud Control.

  • Nexus Hyperfabric — A cloud-managed, AI-driven data center fabric solution for simplified network operations.

  • Cisco Collaboration Control Hub (formerly Webex Control Hub) — The administration portal for managing Webex collaboration services, users, and devices at scale.

Not all products listed above will be actively used in every section of this lab. However, their presence in the topology reflects the breadth of the Cisco Cloud Control platform and the scope of what agentic workflows can reach and act upon.

docs.title: Step 2: Log into the dCloud Cloud Control Lab
docs.text:
Open a web browser and navigate to the lab landing page at: https://dcloud2-rtp.cisco.com/content/instantdemo/agenticops-with-cisco-cloud-control Click View + Answer questions are how you plan to use the demo (new window opens)

Next, Click Login

After logging in, explore the three sections on the home screen.

1. Selected Organization — If you have access to more than one organization, use this section to switch between them.

2. AI Assistant — Use this natural language interface to interact with the platform. Explore the pre-built prompts.

3. Actions — Review any actions required in your environment. Take note of what is displayed. These actions can be engaged agentically, which will be covered in detail later in this lab.

Next, navigate to AI Canvas Prompt Library (opens in new Tab for easy navigation) and spend time running the validated prompts for this environment. Use the copy button on each prompt block to paste directly into the AI Assistant or Agentic Canvas — this ensures accuracy and eliminates the risk of transcription errors. As you work through each prompt, observe how the system interprets the input, what format the response takes, and how quickly results are returned.

The goal of this exercise is to thoroughly prepare yourself for live customer demonstrations by building familiarity and confidence with a core set of prompts that consistently produce clear, accurate, and compelling results. Consider the following as you explore:

  • Identify your strongest examples. Some prompts will generate output that is particularly well-suited for showcasing the capabilities of the environment. Take note of these and prioritize them for use in demos.

  • Understand the output. Be prepared to explain to a customer not just what the output shows, but why it is useful and how it maps to a real-world business scenario or use case.

  • Anticipate follow-up questions. As you review each result, think about questions a customer might ask and ensure you can speak confidently to the underlying functionality.

  • Practice your delivery. Running through these prompts multiple times will help you develop a smooth, natural delivery so that the demonstration feels polished and professional rather than scripted.

Take as much time as needed during this section to become comfortable with the material. A well-rehearsed demonstration using familiar prompts is far more effective than presenting new or untested examples under the pressure of a live customer engagement.

Example prompts you can use:

Tip

You can access AI Canvas Prompt Library (opens in new Tab for easy navigation) at any time from the navigation menu on the left. Each prompt has a copy button — click it to copy the prompt instantly to your clipboard, then paste it directly into the AI Assistant or Agentic Canvas.

Note

Since this environment is integrated with both Meraki and Catalyst Center orgs, for prompts related to the network, you will be prompted to select the correct organization.

How is my organization doing?

Are there any outages affecting my monitored services right now?

What are the current latency and packet loss metrics for my critical tests?

What is the current status of all my site-to-site VPN tunnels?

Example:

Note

Actual responses will vary due to the nature of Agentic Systems

Finally, click on Actions in the AI Assistant. Notice how the agentic system automatically analyzes these actions and correlates the related events for you, eliminating the need for manual investigation. Rather than requiring you to sift through individual log entries or alerts, the AI Assistant groups and connects relevant activities into a cohesive, contextualized narrative — making it significantly easier to understand the full scope and sequence of an incident. See the example below:

Note

Notice that we can also move an Action to "Collaborate in Canvas". We will be exploring the Agentic AI Canvas in the next section.

docs.title: Step 3: Explore 9-Dot Menu
docs.text:
Click the 9-dot menu (grid icon) located in the top navigation bar of Cloud Control to explore the available options and applications.

Explore the three main sections available on the platform.

1. Platform Services — These services span the entire infrastructure. Each will be explored in detail throughout this lab. Additional services, such as Fabric, will continue to be added over time.

2. Products — These are the products currently integrated with your tenant. In a production environment, multiple products would typically be present. For a full list of supported products and onboarding requirements, visit the Cloud Control Onboarding SharePoint site.

3. Apps — Common applications residing in Cloud Control.

4. Favorites — Save frequently visited pages from any product in this section for quick access during future sessions.

Note

Click a Platform Service or Product to pin it to the navigation bar. This bar remains visible throughout Cloud Control, enabling quick and consistent access regardless of where you navigate.

Caution

Due to the scale constraints of this lab, Intersight and Nexus Dashboard products are not available as managed Products.

docs.title: Step 4: Explore Inventory Capabilities
docs.text:
Navigate to the Inventory section of Cisco Cloud Control to explore the available inventory capabilities.

Next, explore the available capabilities. Review the Inventory Insights dashboard to examine detected issues, recommendations, and asset visibility across your managed devices.

Click the alternative view to display the full inventory.

Practice using the AI-assisted search functionality within the Inventory section. Collaborate with your team to explore the available Inventory capabilities, including filtering, sorting, and device categorization options.

1. Enter the sample prompt below into the AI-Assisted Search and press Enter:

show me my Mexico City Devices

2. Click the C9300-X-Leaf-1 switch to view it.

3. Review the device details panel that opens on the right side of the screen. This panel displays comprehensive information for your C9300-X-Leaf-1 switch. Review the General tab, which provides a high-level device overview including key operational indicators. Confirm that the Reachability status shows Reachable, indicating the device is actively communicating with the management platform, and that the Compliance status shows Compliant, confirming the device configuration meets your organisation's defined policy standards.

4. Click View in Topology. This will take you directly to the switch in the Global Topology Service.

The Topology view displays your global network topology organized by site, providing a visual representation of device relationships and connectivity across your environment. In this case, we pivoted directly to the C9300-X-Leaf1 in the local site topology. Notice the navigation options available to go directly to the device in Meraki or pivot back to the device in inventory.

To demonstrate the seamless pivot to the Mexico City network, Click Meraki on the top navigation banner.

This action opens the Meraki Dashboard in context for the selected site, demonstrating the seamless cross-platform navigation capability within Cisco Cloud Control.

This integration allows network administrators to move fluidly between unified inventory management and platform-specific dashboards without separately logging in or searching for the device within Meraki.

Notice the top navigation bar, which reflects the unified Cloud Control interface. Click Home to return to the Cloud Control home screen, or click any other element in the banner to navigate directly to it. These tabs allow you to seamlessly move between management planes within a single dashboard.

Congratulations

Congratulations on completing this section! You have successfully navigated the Cisco Cloud Control platform and gained hands-on experience with its core services, including the AI Assistant, Inventory, Topology, and Actions. These foundational skills will serve as building blocks as you progress through the remaining sections of this lab.

docs.title: Section 2: Experience the Agentic AI Canvas
Section 2: Experience the Agentic AI Canvas
docs.text: In this section we will explore the AI Canvas and Agentic Ops capabilities in Cisco Cloud Control

docs.title: Step 1: Open AI Canvas
docs.text: Start on the Home section by clicking Canvas.

docs.title: Step 2: Explore the AI Canvas Home and Launch a Quick Start
docs.text:
Now in the AI Canvas section you will see:

  1. The ability to create a New Canvas

  2. Integrations, which allow you to add API integrations into Cavas

  3. The Recent list of Canvases

Next, click + New and let's put AI Canvas to work with a new Canvas.

Note

Canvas may prompt you to answer a set of clarifying questions before generating content. These questions are designed to help Canvas better understand your specific requirements, preferences, and goals, ensuring that the output is tailored precisely to your needs. Simply read each question carefully and provide your answers as you see fit. There are no right or wrong responses — your answers serve as guidance to help Canvas produce the most relevant and accurate result possible.

docs.title: Step 3: Explore the Wireless Canvas Session
docs.text:
Next, we will use a built-in Meraki Health & Availability prompt to create a Wireless Health Check.

From the "Where should we begin?" menu:

  1. Select Health & Availability

  2. Select Meraki

  3. Finally, select "Run a WiFi health check on my Meraki networks"

Next, watch closely as AI Canvas generates the Wireless Health Report reviewing wireless performance, clients, and alerts in the environment.

Once it completes, spend some time exploring the various capabilities of the Canvas interface, such as the ability to share and invite others, annotate, resize cards, generate a summary, and more.

docs.title: Step 4: Use Prompt Shortcuts and Reasoning Mode
docs.text:
1. Within Canvas, practice entering / for a set of pre-populated prompts and # for accessing and managing a knowledge base of contextual information.

  2. Notice that you can toggle between Default and Reasoning Mode. See the detailed differences below:

Default Mode uses a standard language model optimized for speed and general-purpose assistance. It is well-suited for everyday tasks, asking quick questions, and getting explanations. Responses are generated quickly, making this mode ideal when you need fast, iterative feedback.

Reasoning Mode leverages a more advanced model capable of multi-step reasoning and complex problem analysis. This mode is better suited for tasks that require careful, methodical thinking, such as:

  • Debugging complex, hard-to-reproduce issues that span multiple systems

  • Working through problems that require the model to plan several steps ahead before producing an answer

Note

The trade-off with Reasoning mode is that responses take longer to generate due to the additional computational steps involved. For straightforward tasks, Default mode will typically be faster and sufficient, while Reasoning mode is most valuable when accuracy and thoroughness outweigh the need for speed.

docs.title: Step 5: Review an AI Canvas Root Cause Analysis Example
docs.text:
Finally, review the example below of using Canvas to arrive at a root cause analysis (RCA) for a given scenario. Due to time constraints, we will NOT be running the prompts below — they are provided for your reference and for when you demo to customers in the future. Please just review the example.

The scenario below involves a Network Operator who wants to perform Root Cause Analysis (RCA) on SD-WAN sites that are down. The progression of prompts used is outlined below, and the screenshots are provided for your reference.

Example sequence of prompts:

Prompt #1 Summarize my Catalyst SD-WAN deployment

Prompt #2 Give me the list of sites with low availability

Prompt #3 I can see that Site_101 has 0% availability. Help me troubleshoot and identify the root cause

Note

Actual responses will vary due to the nature of Agentic Systems

Example screenshots below:

Congratulations

You now have the foundational knowledge required to work effectively with the Agentic AI Canvas. This concludes the section.

docs.title: Section 3: Identity
docs.text: In this section, you will explore Identity Intelligence in Cisco Cloud Control. You will review the identities in the environment — users, endpoints, agents, and non-human identities — and see how trust levels, identity checks, and MFA posture surface risky accounts before they become incidents.

docs.title: Step 1: Open Identity Intelligence and Review the Posture Dashboard
docs.text:
Caution

This is a live lab environment. The identities, counts, scores, and dashboards you see in Identity Intelligence will vary from the screenshots in this guide as data changes over time.

From the Cloud Control top bar, open the 9-Dot Menu and select Identity. The Identity Intelligence Dashboard opens by default.

From the drop down Click the Overview Dashboard (Take note of all the other available dashboards)

The Dashboard answers one question: how healthy is the identity posture of this organization right now?

  • Organization Posture Score — a single 0–100 score (79, Neutral in this lab) rolled up from every identity check across all connected identity sources.

  • Posture score trend — how the score has moved over the selected window (30 days by default), so you can tell whether remediation work is paying off.

  • Top Recommendations — per-category scores for Human Identities, Non-Human Identities, and MFA, each with the single highest-impact fix, how many identities it affects, and the checks that contribute to it.

Tip

Click any users or contributing check link on a recommendation card to jump straight to the filtered list of affected identities.

docs.title: Step 2: Explore Users
docs.text:
In the left navigation, click Users.

Users is a single, correlated inventory of every human identity, regardless of where the account lives. In this lab, accounts from PseudoCo AD, PseudoCo Duo, PseudoCo Entra ID, and PseudoCo ISE are merged into one record per person.

  • Trust Level — whether the identity is Trusted or Unknown based on its behavior and posture.

  • Checks — the number of failing identity checks for that user.

  • # IPs, # Logins, Last Seen, Last IP Address, Last Location — recent authentication activity.

  • MFA and Source — whether MFA is enrolled and which identity providers hold the account.

Use the filter panel on the left (Status, Source, Trust Level, Compiled Status, Lifecycle Events, User Type) to slice the population, and the search bar to find a user by name, group, application, or IP.

Note

Default filters hide deleted, deprovisioned, and disabled accounts. Toggle Default filters off to see the full population.

Next search for the user Alex Garcia. Once found Click to explore the user details in a new tab

Spend time exploring all of the details and capabilities available to the user.

docs.title: Step 3: Explore Applications
docs.text:
Click Applications.

Applications lists every application your identity providers authenticate users into — here, the Duo and Entra ID SSO applications such as Secure Access, dCloud SASE demos, and Jira.

  • Status and # Logins — whether the app is active and actually used (the usage window is 30 days).

  • Sensitive — mark business-critical apps as sensitive; Cloud Control also recommends apps that look sensitive.

  • Tags — risk signals such as Not accessed, No Assignment Required, User Bypass Risk, or Password Expired.

Tip

An app tagged No Assignment Required can be reached by any user in the directory. Combine that tag with Sensitive = Yes to find your highest-risk applications.

docs.title: Step 4: Explore Endpoints
docs.text:
Click Endpoints.

Endpoints shows the devices your users authenticate from, correlated from Duo, Microsoft Entra ID, and Cisco ISE.

  • Managed and Registered — whether the device is under management and registered with an identity provider.

  • OS and OS Status — platform and patch state (Latest, Out of date, End of life).

  • Tags — New, Known, Encrypted, Shared, Owned.

  • Assigned Users — who uses the device, linking device risk back to the identity.

Note

Phone-number device names are masked automatically to protect personal data.

docs.title: Step 5: Explore AI Agents
docs.text:
Click Agents.

AI Agents is the inventory of AI agents operating in your environment, treated as identities in their own right. For each agent you can see its Owner, Sources, Agent Platform, Connected Platforms, Risk level (Critical to Minor), Type, and how it was discovered.

As teams adopt agentic tools, this view answers who owns each agent, what it can reach, and how risky it is.

Note

No AI agents are present in this lab tenant, so the list is empty.

docs.title: Step 6: Explore Non-Human Identities
docs.text:
Click Non-Human Identities.

Non-Human Identities (NHIs) are service accounts, service principals, and agentic apps that authenticate without a person behind them. They are often over-privileged and unowned, which makes them a favorite target.

This lab has one NHI: a PowerPlatform agentic app from Entra ID. Note its failing check and the Humans/Users Assigned column showing N/A: nobody owns it.

Tip

This NHI is the one behind the Dashboard recommendation “Assign owners to non-human identities without an accountable owner.”

docs.title: Step 7: Review Integrations
docs.text:
Click Integrations.

Integrations shows the identity sources that feed Identity Intelligence. This lab connects four providers: PseudoCo AD, PseudoCo Duo, PseudoCo Entra ID, and PseudoCo ISE.

For each one, check Connectivity, Collection Status, Recent Usage, and Last Collected to confirm data is flowing. Every other Identity page is built from these sources.

Caution

Do not add, edit, or remove integrations in this shared lab tenant.

docs.title: Step 8: Explore Identity Checks
docs.text:
Click Checks.

Checks are the continuous tests that drive every score you have seen. Each check shows:

  • Pass rate (the ring), severity (Critical, Moderate, Low), and its scope and topic (for example End Users – Compliance, Identity Posture Insight).

  • # Failing, with the week-over-week and month-over-month trend.

  • Report Channels — where alerts for that check are sent.

Examples in this lab include NHI with No Owners Assigned, Never Logged In, Inactive Users, No MFA Configured, and Admin Role Assigned to User. Use the filters to narrow checks by compatible source, compliance, severity, topic, framework, or scope.

Caution

Leave Run checks now, the enable toggles, and Report Channels unchanged in this shared tenant.

docs.title: Step 9: Monitor ISE Health
docs.text:
Click ISE Monitoring.

The ISE Health Dashboard (Beta) monitors the on-premises Cisco ISE deployment through a lightweight ISE Agent:

  • ISE Agent — connection status, last heartbeat, uptime, agent version, and whether an update is available.

  • Deployment — ISE version and patch, admin IP, node count, active sessions, and average authentication latency.

  • Auth Latency and Active Sessions charts for the last 24 hours.

This brings on-prem ISE health into the same cloud console as the rest of your identity estate.

docs.title: Step 10: Audit Activity in System Logs
docs.text:
Click System Logs.

System Logs is the audit trail for Identity Intelligence: integration data uploads, admin-triggered actions such as integration tests, check runs, and AI requests. Each event records its Initiator, Target, Result, and the component that logged it.

Filter by Result (for example Failure or Timeout) or Event Family (Integrations, User checks, Admin triggered) to troubleshoot collection problems or see who changed what.

Congratulations

You have completed the Identity section. You toured the full Identity Intelligence workflow: posture scoring, human and non-human identity inventories, applications and endpoints, the checks behind every score, ISE health, and the audit trail.

docs.title: Section 4: Splunk Secure Networking App
docs.text: In this section, you will explore Splunk Secure Networking Essentials (SSNE), the Splunk app built into Cisco Cloud Control. SSNE correlates telemetry from Cisco ISE, Duo, Secure Access, Secure Firewall, Meraki, Catalyst Center, Catalyst SD-WAN, Nexus Dashboard, ACI, ThousandEyes, XDR, and AI Defense into executive workspaces and investigation dashboards organized around five secure-networking pillars: Zero Trust Access, Secure Infrastructure, Scalable Network Segmentation, Hybrid Mesh Firewalling, and Agentic Ops.

docs.title: Step 1: Launch Splunk Secure Networking Essentials
docs.text:
From the Cloud Control top bar, open the 9-Dot Menu and click Splunk. Splunk Cloud opens inside Cloud Control on the Splunk Secure Networking Essentials Insights Workspace.

The Insights Workspace is the executive starting point for the whole app:

  • Headline tiles — one health signal per pillar, each with a status badge (Healthy, Warning, Critical): ZTA auth failure rate, DC critical anomalies, active SGT assignments, Hybrid Mesh Firewall blocked flows, degraded digital paths, and Palo Alto policy blocks.

  • Pillar rows — collapsible Zero Trust Access, Secure Infrastructure, and other rows of trend tiles. Page through them with the arrows, or change how many tiles show per page.

  • Secure Network Command Map — live sites, trust paths, and policy-enforcement health on a geographic map (switch to Table for a list), with inter-site and site-link availability below it.

  • Controls — layout toggles, time range (default Last 24 hours), and refresh rate.

The left navigation groups every dashboard by pillar. Click a pillar to open a menu of its dashboards.

Tip

Click the open icon on any headline tile to jump straight to the dashboard behind that number.

docs.title: Step 2: Zero Trust Access
docs.text: In the left navigation, click Zero Trust Access. A menu slides out listing this pillar's dashboards; open each one in turn by clicking it in the menu. This pillar answers: are the right users and devices getting access, and are policies being enforced?

docs.title: Zero Trust Posture
docs.text:
Click Zero Trust Access in the left navigation, then click Zero Trust Posture in the menu.

The pillar summary. It connects identity, posture, policy, and response signals across the access journey: ISE Authentication Outcomes and Friction (failure rate), Secure Access ZTNA Private Access Status, Remote Access Health, Duo Risky MFA Outcomes ranked by application and factor, and Control Telemetry Volume from ISE, ZTNA, and FMC.

docs.title: Authentication and Policy Enforcement
docs.text:
Click Zero Trust Access again to reopen the menu, then click Authentication and Policy Enforcement.

Validates that authentication works and policy is applied: ISE failure rate, RADIUS vs TACACS+ Policy Family Activity, RADIUS Outcomes, RadSec Transport Activity, Duo Policy Outcomes (denied, success, fraud), and the ISE Enforcement Footprint — how many network access devices are actively enforcing.

docs.title: Policy Management
docs.text:
Click Zero Trust Access again to reopen the menu, then click Policy Management.

Monitors access-policy coverage, change, and exceptions that need review: RADIUS enforcement, secure transport, MFA policy outcomes, ZTNA Denial Reasons (which policy, posture, certificate, or connector reason is blocking users), and TrustSec SGACL Enforcement.

docs.title: User Activity Monitoring
docs.text:
Click Zero Trust Access again to reopen the menu, then click User Activity Monitoring.

Reveals unusual access behavior and the identities, devices, and resources involved: private application access, access denial causes, MFA activity, and — from endpoint telemetry — User and Process Egress Concentration, which rank the users and processes sending the most data out.

docs.title: Detection & Response
docs.text:
Click Zero Trust Access again to reopen the menu, then click Detection & Response.

Surfaces access-related detections and the response actions that contain risk: Cisco XDR Incident Severity and Incident Risk Pressure, Attack Analyzer flows and forensic detections, External Egress Activity by destination, and File Source Hotspots.

docs.title: Remote Access VPN (RaVPN) Sessions and Posture
docs.text:
Click Zero Trust Access again to reopen the menu, then click Remote Access VPN (RaVPN) Sessions and Posture.

Connects remote-session health with endpoint posture and access risk: VPN clients and sessions, connection outcomes, VPN profiles and regions in use, ranked Failure Reasons, and Posture Outcomes (non-compliant, failed, warning).

Note

Each panel shows its data domain and pillar under the title (for example Identity · Zero Trust Access), and its description states exactly what is — and is not — being counted.

docs.title: Step 3: Secure Infrastructure
docs.text: In the left navigation, click Secure Infrastructure. A menu slides out listing this pillar's dashboards; open each one in turn by clicking it in the menu. This pillar answers: is the network and data center healthy, and where is it exposed?

docs.title: Secure Infrastructure Status
docs.text:
Click Secure Infrastructure in the left navigation, then click Secure Infrastructure Status in the menu.

One cross-source health view of wireless, Catalyst Center, SD-WAN, data center, endpoint, and firewall: Meraki Reporting Access Points, Catalyst Active Issues, Reporting SD-WAN Sites, Nexus Dashboard Data Center Signals, Secure Endpoint Endpoint Incidents, and FMC Firewall Activity.

docs.title: Infrastructure Posture
docs.text:
Click Secure Infrastructure again to reopen the menu, then click Infrastructure Posture.

Unifies assurance, exposure, and operational control signals: data center anomalies, Nexus Dashboard Critical Advisories, Meraki Wireless Containment of rogue access points, Wireless Clients Observed, and SD-WAN site reporting.

docs.title: Secure Data Center Operations
docs.text:
Click Secure Infrastructure again to reopen the menu, then click Secure Data Center Operations.

Fabric health, capacity, policy enforcement, runtime security, and change intelligence for ACI, APIC, Nexus Dashboard, Secure Firewall, and Cisco Isovalent. Tabs across the top switch between Fabric Operations, Data Center Security, Runtime Security, and Runtime Investigation. Fabric Operations shows the ACI Fabric Health Score, critical and major ACI faults, security advisories, interface anomalies, peak port utilization, and ACI configuration changes.

docs.title: SD-WAN and Network Health Monitoring
docs.text:
Click Secure Infrastructure again to reopen the menu, then click SD-WAN and Network Health Monitoring.

Correlates WAN health, reachability, and service impact: SD-WAN Site Health, Circuit Availability, Degraded Tunnels, Application Health, and ThousandEyes Path Loss and BGP Routing Stability.

Note

Panels with no data in the selected window say so explicitly and suggest checking that the data source is onboarded or widening the time range.

docs.title: Step 4: Scalable Network Segmentation
docs.text: In the left navigation, click Scalable Network Segmentation. A menu slides out listing this pillar's dashboards; open each one in turn by clicking it in the menu. This pillar answers: how far has TrustSec/SGT segmentation been adopted, and is it being enforced?

docs.title: Segmentation Readiness
docs.text:
Click Scalable Network Segmentation in the left navigation, then click Segmentation Readiness in the menu.

Connects segmentation posture, trust boundaries, and enforcement coverage: the TrustSec-capable Hardware Inventory, endpoint-to-SGT assignments, which Security Groups are in use, the Segmentation Adoption Rate, Sites With No Observed SGT Coverage, and tagged authentication events by location.

docs.title: Segmentation Operations
docs.text:
Click Scalable Network Segmentation again to reopen the menu, then click Segmentation Operations.

Summarizes segment health, policy alignment, and areas needing investigation: tagged endpoints by reporting device, IP-SGT Bindings, SGACL Decisions (permit, deny), VRF / VLAN / VXLAN / SGT feature events, and FMC Blocks by SGT Context — where firewall policy is acting on group tags.

Tip

Use Sites With No Observed SGT Coverage as a rollout checklist: each listed site authenticates users but never assigns a non-default Security Group Tag.

docs.title: Step 5: Hybrid Mesh Firewalling
docs.text: In the left navigation, click Hybrid Mesh Firewalling. A menu slides out listing this pillar's dashboards; open each one in turn by clicking it in the menu. This pillar answers: is policy enforced consistently across every firewall — on-prem, branch, cloud, and workload?

docs.title: Hybrid Mesh Enforcement
docs.text:
Click Hybrid Mesh Firewalling in the left navigation, then click Hybrid Mesh Enforcement in the menu.

Unifies firewall posture, enforcement, and workload protection: Reporting Firewalls, Unified Block Activity across Meraki MX and Secure Firewall/ASA, FMC enforcement, Umbrella/SSE DNS Security Activity, Palo Alto SGT-tagged Policy Decisions, and Secure Access DLP findings.

docs.title: Threat Detection and Enforcement
docs.text:
Click Hybrid Mesh Firewalling again to reopen the menu, then click Threat Detection and Enforcement.

Tracks high-confidence detections and the controls enforcing policy: allowed vs blocked Firewall Decisions, Cloud Firewall Blocks, the Multicloud Defense Deny Rate, Isovalent Runtime Alerts, Branch IPS Pressure from SD-WAN UTD, and a unified enforcement trend.

docs.title: DLP and Cloud Native Security
docs.text:
Click Hybrid Mesh Firewalling again to reopen the menu, then click DLP and Cloud Native Security.

Exposes data-loss risk and cloud-native workload controls: Data Loss Findings by severity, Secure Workload Workload Alert Pressure, the cloud enforcement rate, runtime detection severity, and native AWS / Azure / GCP Cloud Security Activity.

docs.title: Step 6: Agentic Ops
docs.text: In the left navigation, click Agentic Ops. A menu slides out listing this pillar's dashboards; open each one in turn by clicking it in the menu. This pillar answers: are users getting a good digital experience, and what should operators and executives act on first?

docs.title: Operational Intelligence
docs.text:
Click Agentic Ops in the left navigation, then click Operational Intelligence in the menu.

Coordinates test health, path quality, routing instability, and AI Defense signals: Degraded ThousandEyes Tests with a table of tests needing attention, AI Defense Policy Outcomes (blocked vs allowed prompts), latency by reporting agent, network loss, lowest application availability, and BGP path changes by test.

docs.title: Secure Networking Assurance
docs.text:
Click Agentic Ops again to reopen the menu, then click Secure Networking Assurance.

Rolls protected-application access into one decision-ready Secure Networking Assurance Score built from Attainability (ThousandEyes HTTP availability), Retainability (ISE and ZTNA success), and Quality (latency and packet loss), adjusted by a Contextual risk multiplier from active XDR incidents.

docs.title: Executive Assurance
docs.text:
Click Agentic Ops again to reopen the menu, then click Executive Assurance.

Summarizes posture, operational risk, and business-relevant outcomes for leadership: Fleet Device Health, lowest site connectivity, wireless availability, identity friction, reported enforcement blocks, and lowest application availability.

Note

If the assurance score shows N/A, one of its inputs had no data in the selected window. Widen the time range to see the trend.

docs.title: Step 7: Investigate Any Panel
docs.text:
Every panel has two icons in its top-right corner:

  • ⓘ — what the panel measures and how to read it.

  • Search (magnifier) — opens the panel's exact search, with the active time range, in Splunk Search, so you can pivot from any number to the raw events behind it.

Use the Time range buttons (4h, 24h, 48h, 7d, 30d) at the top of each dashboard to change the window.

Congratulations

You have completed the Splunk Secure Networking App section. You explored the Insights Workspace and all five secure-networking pillars, and learned how to drill from any metric to its underlying search.

docs.title: Section 5: Studio
docs.text: Cisco Cloud Control Studio is the extensibility, governance, and customization engine of the Cisco Cloud Control platform. Part of Cisco's AgenticOps strategy, it gives IT and security operations teams a design space to build autonomous AI agents and applications that bridge Cisco infrastructure and third-party tools. In this section, you will use its two environments — App Builder and Agent Builder — and see how everything built in Studio is governed by AI Defense guardrails, traced through Splunk AI Agent Monitoring, and published for use across the platform.

docs.title: Step 1: Open Cloud Control Studio
docs.text:
From the Cloud Control top bar, open the 9-Dot Menu and, under Platform Services, click Studio.

Studio has two tabs:

  • Build — start something new. Choose an Agent, which runs on demand or when triggered to monitor conditions, investigate issues, and automate work, or an App, which opens from the Apps menu and brings together dashboards, forms, visualizations, and guided workflows.

  • Manage — every agent and app you have built, with its type, status, and version.

You will build an agent first, then an app.

docs.title: Step 2: Shape an Agent with Agent Builder
docs.text:
On the Agent card, click Build.

Agent Builder lets you engineer an AI agent for your own workflows, troubleshooting paths, and policies by describing the behavior you want in natural language — no code required. Quick start prompts give you a head start: Meraki operations and Secure Access operations.

The recommended Meraki operations prompt is already filled in: Build a Meraki operations agent that reviews alerts and device health, prioritizes issues, and sends a concise report every day at 9:00 AM Pacific. Click the Build arrow to submit it.

Note

This lab environment runs approved prompts only, so you build from the recommended or Quick start prompts. In your own tenant you can describe any agent you need.

docs.title: Step 3: Watch Studio Build the Agent and Review Its Manifest
docs.text:
Studio turns your description into a working agent. Watch the build progress through Reviewing your request, Preparing the conversation, and Updating your Agent, where it connects the agent's capabilities.

In under a minute the draft is ready and saved as version v1. Review the generated Agent manifest on the Review Agent tab:

  • Agent name and description — Studio generates the name from your prompt, so yours may differ slightly — for example, Meraki Daily Operations Review or Daily Meraki Operations Report.

  • Instructions — the agent's operating rules, written from your prompt. Note the built-in boundaries: Do not invent thresholds, findings, or remediation actions, and clearly call out missing, stale, or unavailable data.

  • MCP servers — meraki-server. Agents reach Cisco and third-party tools (such as AWS, ServiceNow, PagerDuty, and Wiz) through native APIs or the open Model Context Protocol (MCP).

  • Trigger and schedule — scheduled execution at cron(0 16 * * ? *) (16:00 UTC, 9:00 AM Pacific), with a scheduled-run prompt and a run limit.

Tip

Repetitive operational logic and diagnostic routines can be encoded as reusable agent skills, so every agent you build can call them instead of re-learning them.

docs.title: Step 4: Test the Agent in the Sandbox
docs.text:
Before an agent runs on its own, you test it in the Sandbox with a prompt that describes the task — exactly what it will be asked to do on its schedule.

  1. In the Review and Test panel on the right, click the Test tab.

  2. Click in the Scenario box and enter the test prompt: Run the daily Meraki operations review and report the highest-priority issues first.

  1. Click Run scenario.

The agent works through four stages, shown under Scenario execution progress:

  • Understanding the scenario — interprets your prompt against its instructions.

  • Gathering permitted context — calls only the tools it has been granted, here the Meraki MCP server.

  • Applying guardrails — AI Defense checks the run against policy before anything is returned.

  • Preparing the result — assembles the report.

  1. Wait for Scenario Result: Completed (about one to three minutes), then read the report.

The agent returns a prioritized operations report covering the last 24 hours. Notice how it is structured:

  • Grouped by severity — 🔴 Critical, 🟠 High, and 🟡 Medium sections, highest first, as the prompt asked.

  • Evidence — the data behind each finding, such as both Bangalore fabric border nodes losing their default routes.

  • Next Check — a concrete action for the operator, including the exact CLI commands to run and when to escalate to TAC.

Note

Actual responses will vary due to the nature of the Live Lab environment and Agentic Systems

  1. Scroll down to review the High and Medium findings and the Meraki Fleet Summary at the end.

Where data could not be retrieved, the agent says so — for example, it reports the organization health score as unavailable rather than inventing one. That behavior comes straight from the instructions in its manifest.

Tip

Run the test again with a different scenario — for example, Only report issues affecting the Mexico City network — to see how the same agent adapts to a new request within its guardrails.

docs.title: Publishing the agent
docs.text:
After a successful test, you would publish the agent. Publishing moves it out of Draft and makes it available for use across Cloud Control, where it runs on its schedule.

Caution

Publishing is not available in this lab. Due to permissions in the dCloud environment, you cannot publish the agent here. The agent stays in Draft.

Note

The agent only gathers permitted context, and AI Defense guardrails are applied to every run — they enforce what data the agent can see and which actions require human approval. A successful test also enables the agent's scheduling actions.

docs.title: Step 5: Generate an App with App Builder
docs.text:
Click Build (top left) to return to Studio, and on the App card click Build.

App Builder generates and publishes custom operational applications from natural-language requirements. Each Quick start attaches a pre-built requirements file (.md): Golden Image Compliance, Unified Software and Advisory Attention, and Connected Clients and VPN Sessions.

Keep the recommended prompt — Create an app according to the requirements in the attached golden-image-compliance.md file — and click the Build arrow.

Studio first turns the requirements into a build plan — who the app is for, the primary experience, the UI family, the rationale, the actions and states it must handle, and the summaries it should show — then builds the app from that approved plan.

Note

An app build takes several minutes. Studio's embedded agentic coding assistant writes the code, tests it, and fixes failures before declaring the build complete.

docs.title: Step 6: Review the Generated App
docs.text:
When the build completes, Studio summarizes what it built and how it was verified, and the live app appears in Preview.

Note

Actual responses will vary due to the nature of the Live Lab environment and Agentic Systems

For Golden Image Compliance, Studio built:

  • Live Meraki and Intersight discovery and evidence enrichment.

  • Reconciled compliance metrics — an Assurance snapshot of live, assessed, compliant, non-compliant, and exception counts — plus Product data coverage per source.

  • Filtering, an evidence drawer, a Policy catalog, Generate report (monthly CSV), and Refresh devices.

  • Truthful loading, empty, partial, stale, and unavailable states — when a source cannot be read, the app says so instead of showing misleading numbers.

The generated code passed its full verification gate — 76 tests, type checking, lint, a governance guard, and a production build — before it was handed back to you.

Tip

Use the navigation on the left of the preview to drill into the Meraki and Intersight workspaces. You have extended Cloud Control with a new, purpose-built application without writing any code.

Caution

Publishing is not available in this lab. Due to permissions in the dCloud environment, you cannot publish the app here. The app stays in Draft.

docs.title: Step 7: Update with Natural Language, Then Publish
docs.text: An app or agent is never finished on the first pass. To change it, you simply describe the change in the Studio prompt box — for example, add a site filter or also check Catalyst Center devices — and Studio updates the plan, regenerates and re-tests the code, and saves a new version.

docs.title: What publishing does
docs.text:
When you are satisfied, click Install to publish the app. Publishing takes the app out of Draft and makes it available to everyone in your organization from the Cloud Control 9-Dot Menu, under Apps — right alongside the built-in Cisco products. Everything built in Studio can also be versioned and packaged to the Cisco Cloud Control Marketplace for deployment across multi-tenant environments.

Note

In this lab, prompt editing is disabled (approved prompts only), so natural-language updates are described rather than performed. Publishing is also unavailable due to permissions in the dCloud environment, so the agent and app you built remain in Draft.

Click Build to return to Studio, then click the Manage tab.

Manage Applications lists everything you have built — here the Meraki operations agent and the Golden Image Compliance app, both in Draft — with filters for scope, capability, and status.

docs.title: Governed by design
docs.text:
• AI Defense and guardrails — continuous runtime scanning enforces what data an agent or app can see and which actions require mandatory human approval.

  • Splunk AI Agent Monitoring — every agent execution path is traced, auditable, and recorded in unified logs underpinned by Cisco Data Fabric.

  • Dual execution modes — custom agents can join AI Canvas investigations alongside human operators, or run continuously in the background as ambient agents that flag infrastructure exceptions — like the scheduled Meraki agent you just built.

Congratulations

You have completed the Studio section. You built and tested an AI agent with Agent Builder, generated a tested application with App Builder, and learned how Studio keeps everything you build governed, monitored, and ready to publish.

docs.title: Section 6: Cloud Control and Cisco IQ
Section 6: Cloud Control and Cisco IQ
docs.text: In this section, you will see how Cisco IQ and Cisco Cloud Control work together. Cisco IQ continuously assesses your Cisco estate for security advisories, configuration and hardening gaps, certificate expiry, and quantum readiness. When IQ is connected, those findings enrich the Cloud Control inventory right where operators already work, and a single click takes you to the exact device in Cisco IQ. You will follow one device from an inventory insight, through its IQ assessments, to an AI Canvas conversation that explains how to fix what IQ found.

docs.title: Step 1: Spot the Quantum Readiness Insight in Inventory
docs.text:
Caution

This is a live lab environment. The devices, counts, and findings you see will vary from the screenshots in this guide as data changes over time.

In the Cloud Control top bar, click Inventory.

The Insights row surfaces the issues that matter most across every connected platform. Look for Devices that don't pass quantum readiness assessments — a Critical insight that comes from Cisco IQ, not from a network controller. Because IQ is connected, its assessment results show up here automatically.

docs.title: Step 2: Filter to the Affected Devices
docs.text:
On the quantum readiness insight card, click Show devices.

Inventory filters to the devices behind the insight and explains why they match: their Cisco IQ quantum readiness assessment total is greater than zero. The table already shows IQ data — note the Security Advisories column with critical (C) and high (H) counts per device.

Tip

You can also filter by describing what you want — use Search with AI using natural language above the table, or the suggested filters such as Show assets with critical security advisories.

docs.title: Step 3: Open the Device and Review Cisco IQ Enrichment
docs.text:
Click the ISR4431/K9 router to open its information panel, then expand Asset coverage and support.

A controller can tell you whether a device is healthy and reachable. Cisco IQ adds the context a controller alone can't:

  • Coverage status, Contract number, Support tier (here, Signature), and Coverage end date.

  • Warranty type and Warranty end date — this router's standard warranty ended years ago.

  • Importance, Sold by partner, and when IQ last collected data through its Data connector.

docs.title: Step 4: Review the Cisco IQ Assessments
docs.text:
In the device panel, click the Assessments tab.

This is every Cisco IQ assessment for the device, summarized by severity:

  • Security Advisories — known Cisco PSIRT advisories that affect this hardware and software.

  • Security Hardening — configuration that weakens the device's security posture.

  • Quantum Readiness — how prepared the device is for post-quantum cryptography.

  • Configuration — deviations from Cisco configuration best practices.

  • Certificates — expired and soon-to-expire certificates.

An operator sees all of this without leaving Cloud Control.

docs.title: Step 5: Cross-Launch into Cisco IQ
docs.text:
At the bottom of the Assessments tab, click View in Cisco IQ.

Cisco IQ opens directly on this device's Asset Findings page — no searching, and no second sign-in. The Summary tab shows the same asset details you saw in Cloud Control, plus charts for each assessment. The tabs across the top let you drill into any of them.

Note

Cisco IQ is a separate service. If your lab login does not have Cisco IQ access, review the IQ screenshots in the next three steps instead, then continue with AI Canvas.

docs.title: Step 6: Investigate Quantum Readiness
docs.text:
Click the Quantum Readiness tab.

Quantum computing introduces two threats security teams are only beginning to plan for:

  • Harvest now, decrypt later — encrypted traffic captured today and decrypted once a capable quantum computer exists.

  • Trust now, forge later — the signatures behind today's hardware and software integrity checks, such as Secure Boot, could someday be forged to load malicious firmware.

Cisco IQ evaluates the device against three pillars — Quantum Safe Communications, Quantum Safe Products, and Crypto Agility — and gives an overall Device Quantum Safe Status. For this router it is Hardware refresh required. The Cryptographic Bill of Materials lists the TLS, MACsec, and SSH algorithms actually in use, discovered from show-command output.

Tip

Quantum readiness is a planning tool: it helps make sure the hardware bought this year won't need to be ripped out again in three.

docs.title: Step 7: Check Certificate Expiry and Security Hardening
docs.text:
Click the Certificates tab.

IQ analyzes every certificate on the device. Here, the device certificate has already expired (Critical) and a second expires within 30 days (High). On a VPN edge router, an expired certificate can take tunnels down — exactly the kind of 3 a.m. page a NOC wants to prevent.

Now click the Security Hardening tab.

Every hardening rule is evaluated against the device's configuration and marked Passed, Didn't pass, Inconclusive, or Not applicable. Note VTY Transport Protocol — Didn't pass. You will fix it in the next steps, and because it can be changed in the same maintenance window as the certificate, one outage window closes two problems.

docs.title: Step 8: Ask AI Canvas About Hardening Opportunities
docs.text:
Return to Cloud Control (use the Cloud Control top bar or your browser's back button — you stay signed in). Click Home, open Canvas, and start a New canvas.

In the message box, enter: What security hardening opportunities are on ISR4431/K9?

AI Canvas queries Cisco IQ's assessment data and adds a table to the canvas — the failing hardening findings for the device, summarized by severity, with each rule and what it found. No report to run and no configuration to read line by line.

To read the whole table, hover over the table card and click Enter fullscreen mode (the expand icon at the top right of the card). The summary shows how many findings are High, Medium, and Low, and the rows are sorted by severity.

Scroll inside the table to see the Medium findings — logging, proxy ARP, enable secret, login banner, SSH version, and more.

Scroll to the bottom for the remaining Medium and Low findings, then close fullscreen with the X.

Note

Actual responses will vary due to the nature of the Live Lab environment and Agentic Systems

docs.title: Step 9: Get Remediation Guidance in the Same Conversation
docs.text:
In the same canvas, ask: How do I harden VTY Transport Protocol on ISR4431/K9?

AI Canvas explains the finding before it gives a fix. It shows the rule's impact and description, then the context of what was found on this specific device — which VTY line ranges allow Telnet.

Scroll down. Option 1 gives the Cisco-recommended commands to restrict every VTY range on this device to SSH only — already filled in with the device's actual line numbers.

Keep scrolling. Option 1 finishes with VTY line 15, and Option 2 begins — it covers TTY lines that aren't used for reverse-console connections.

Scroll again to see the rest of Option 2, followed by Important Notes — for example, confirm SSH is configured before removing Telnet, or you could lose management access.

The response ends with a disclaimer and a link back to the Cisco IQ finding detail, and offers to help with the next high-severity finding.

Note

Actual responses will vary due to the nature of the Live Lab environment and Agentic Systems

Caution

Remediation steps are AI-generated. Review and test them in a lab or maintenance window before applying them to a production device. Do not apply configuration changes to devices in this lab.

docs.title: From guidance to action with Cisco Workflows
docs.text:
AI Canvas doesn't have to stop at guidance. Through an MCP integration with Cisco Workflows, it can hand the fix to an automation workflow. In the same canvas, ask: Can you execute the VTY line hardening workflow?

AI Canvas routes the request to the Workflows Agent (Beta). Expand steps completed to see which agent handled it. The agent responds with a Review workflow card for VTY Configuration Hardening — Enforces SSH on VTY Lines — listing exactly what the workflow will do before anything runs.

The workflow has three steps: log in to the device, enter configuration mode and harden VTY access for SSH, and validate the VTY configuration. Nothing changes until an operator clicks Initiate workflow — the human stays in control of every change.

Caution

Running workflows is not available in this lab. This is a limitation of the dCloud lab environment, not of the product: lab accounts are not given permission to execute automated workflows, and this access is not available on request. When you click Initiate workflow, the Workflows Agent returns an access-denied response, and no change is made to the device.

In a customer's own Cloud Control tenant, users who have been granted workflow permissions can click Initiate workflow and the workflow runs end to end — logging in to the device, applying the SSH-only VTY configuration, and validating the result.

Click Initiate workflow anyway to see how the agent handles it. AI Canvas sends Yes, proceed with workflow "VTY Configuration Hardening" on your behalf, and the Workflows Agent checks your permissions before it touches the device.

The agent stops and explains why the workflow couldn't run. Its suggested next steps include contacting an administrator for workflow permissions — ignore that suggestion in this lab. Workflow execution is not available to lab accounts in the dCloud environment, and no one needs to request it. The response also repeats the commands it already generated for this device, which is how an operator would apply the change manually.

The response ends with the full SSH-only VTY configuration for this device and offers to help with the next high-severity finding.

This is the governance model at work: the agent can find, explain, and propose a fix, but it only executes a change when the person asking has permission to make it. In a production tenant with workflow access, the same click runs the three workflow steps and validates the result.

Note

Actual responses will vary due to the nature of the Live Lab environment and Agentic Systems

In one conversation you went from what's wrong, to how to fix it, to an approved, repeatable workflow that applies the fix — without opening another tool or a CLI session. You can also Share the canvas with your on-call operations team so they can review the change before it runs.

Congratulations

You have completed the Cloud Control and Cisco IQ section. You followed a device from an inventory insight to its Cisco IQ assessments, planned for a long-term quantum readiness risk, and used AI Canvas to understand and fix today's hardening risk in a single conversation.

docs.title: Turning Capability into Outcomes
docs.text:
Sections 1 and 2 showed you what Cisco Cloud Control is and how AI Canvas works. The next four sections focus on value realization: seeing how the platform turns what you already own into measurable results.

Cisco customers have invested in identity, security, networking, and observability tools, but much of that value stays locked inside separate consoles. Cloud Control brings those signals together, so teams find risk sooner, resolve issues faster, and act on the same context instead of switching between products. It also lets organizations extend the platform with their own agents and apps, so each new use case builds on the investment they have already made.

As you work through the next sections, look for the value story in each one:

  • Identity — one view of human and non-human identities and their posture, so risky accounts surface before they become incidents.
  • Splunk Secure Networking App — security and network telemetry correlated into dashboards that show where the network is healthy and where it is exposed.
  • Studio — agents and apps built in natural language, extending Cloud Control to fit how each team works, with AI Defense guardrails built in.
  • Cloud Control and Cisco IQ — lifecycle, compliance, and security intelligence that turns findings into a prioritized, actionable fix.

Each of these is a conversation you can have with a customer about the return they get from Cisco Cloud Control.
